summary: Dixon sits in the dead center of the Sacramento Valley's agricultural floor, surrounded by row crops and open sky in every direction — no foothills, no ridgelines, just an unbroken horizon that delivers some of the most dramatic sunsets in inland Northern California, the kind that light up the entire western sky above tomato and sunflower fields. That flatness defines daily life: the city is compact at just 7.2 square miles, bikeable in a way that many California towns aren't, with Interstate 80 running along its southern edge connecting it to Sacramento (about 25 miles east) and the Bay Area (roughly 70 miles southwest). Dixon functions largely as a bedroom community — most employment gravitates toward Sacramento, Davis, or Vacaville — though agriculture and food processing remain significant local employers, and the annual Dixon May Fair is one of the oldest county fairs in California. At a median household income near $99K and a median home price around $576K, the price-to-income ratio lands just under 6:1 — noticeably more accessible than Bay Area cities but still requiring meaningful income to buy. With nearly 9.7 hours of daily sunshine on average, summers run hot (highs well into the 90s) while winters stay mild, and the low 8.4% poverty rate reflects a working, wage-earning economic base rather than a tech-wealth one. Dixon is the rare small California city where the commute buys you space and sky, but the tradeoff is that almost everything beyond groceries and essentials requires getting in a car.
